column4: After Musa's anger subsides, he takes the tablets, whose inscription contains guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord; this joins the anger scene to the guided, forgiven path.
The verse says people exchanged God's favor (نِعْمَتَ اللَّهِ) for disbelief and brought their people to ruin; it directly stages bestowed favor reversed into an adverse end.
The next verse names Hell as the destination of those who brought their people to ruin; it completes the consequence begun in 14:28.
They set up rivals to lead people away from God's path; this connects the rejection of favor in 14:28 with the section's lost-way group.
The secure town had provision from every direction, then denied God's favors and was made to taste hunger and fear; it is a precise provision-to-reversal scene.
A messenger came to that town and its people denied him, so punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers; this completes the preceding reversal.
God says that belief and mindfulness would have opened blessings from heaven and earth, but denial led to seizure; it directly links response to favor with the opposite outcome.

Angels descend upon those who say their Lord is God and remain steadfast (تَتَنَزَّلُ عَلَيْهِمُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ), telling them not to fear or grieve; this is a close positive counterpart to anger descending upon a group.
The descending angels say they are the believers' allies in this life and the next, and announce the Garden; this specifies the favor of the descent in 41:30.
The angels promise forgiveness and noble provision; this completes the favorable message in 41:30–31.
In the same infant-Musa story, Pharaoh's wife calls him a comfort to her eyes (قُرَّتَ عَيْنٍ); it is another exact use of the eye-coolness sense named in the section.
God's anger is stated against hypocrites and idolaters, with Hell prepared for them; this is a distinct group judgment matching the section's anger-and-destination side.
The condemned followed what angered God and disliked His pleasure (أَسْخَطَ اللَّهَ ... وَكَرِهُوا رِضْوَانَهُ); this directly joins the section's anger/pleasure opposition to a chosen course.
The verse says they incurred anger upon anger (بَاءُوا بِغَضَبٍ عَلَىٰ غَضَبٍ) for rejecting what God revealed; it is a repeated formulation of anger settling on a group.
The verse says God's anger is upon people who take disbelievers as allies and that they will abide in punishment; it connects anger to conduct and lasting outcome.
The believers are told not to ally with a people God has angered, who have despaired of the Hereafter; it links the same anger-group to its lost expectation of the final day.
Humiliation is laid upon a people and they incur anger from God for disbelief and rebellion; this repeats the section's combination of an imposed mark and divine anger.

One foundation seeks God's pleasure (رِضْوَانٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ), while the other is on a crumbling bank that collapses with its builder into Hell; this links pleasure with a steady course and its opposite with falling.
A person gives himself seeking God's pleasure (ابْتِغَاءَ مَرْضَاتِ اللَّهِ); this is a specific path of seeking the acceptance that the section contrasts with anger.

The warning to disbelievers describes water that scalds faces and calls it an evil drink (بِئْسَ الشَّرَابُ); this joins the section's face-mark image to its dictionary contrast between commendation and blame.
The next verse promises that believers who do good will not lose their reward; it supplies the other side of the choice introduced in 18:29.
The believers receive the Garden, and the verse calls their reward excellent (نِعْمَ الثَّوَابُ); alongside 18:29's bi'sa, it directly realizes the section's secondary ni'ma/bi'sa contrast.
The verse names the Day of Judgment (يَوْمَ الدِّينِ) again; its question about what that day is makes the section's yawm word and accountability sense explicit.
On that day no soul can do anything for another, and command belongs to God; this specifies the judgment-day boundary named in 82:18.
The chapter identifies the faces covered with dust and darkness in 80:40–41 as those of disbelievers and evildoers; it names the group represented by that adverse facial sign.
On the Day of Resurrection, just scales are set up and no soul is wronged; this gives a concrete judgment-day scene for the section's yawm and two-outcome frame.
God tells Musa that He has tested his people and that Samiri led them astray; this identifies the lost-way cause immediately before Musa returns angry in 20:86.
After an earthquake seizes the appointed group, Musa asks God to forgive them and show mercy; this continues the section's anger, punishment, and pardon themes in the same narrative.
Musa asks for good in this life and the next, and God says His mercy encompasses all things; the verse extends the plea for mercy into a stated divine gift.
The successful are those who follow the Messenger and the light sent down with him; this makes following guidance the route into the mercy described in 7:156.
God says He found the Prophet wandering and guided him (ضَالًّا فَهَدَىٰ); this is a compact reversal from lost direction to bestowed guidance.
God says He found the Prophet needy and enriched him; it pairs provision with the guidance in 93:7, matching the section's joined favor-and-path imagery.
When provision is expanded, a person says his Lord has honored him; this gives a specific case of reading outward provision as favor.
When provision is restricted, the person says his Lord has humiliated him; paired with 89:15, it exposes a mistaken equation between material state and divine standing.
The answer begins “No!” and reproaches them for not honoring the orphan; this marks a boundary against treating abundance or deprivation alone as proof of approval or anger.
The passage names the companions of the right as one group at the event; it is a specific parallel to the section's final division into communities.
The next group is the companions of the left; the right/left pairing supplies a distinct two-group formulation, though the same chapter also names a third group.
The chapter asks about the companions of the right and describes their garden's shade and fruit; this gives the favorable group's embodied outcome.
The chapter asks about the companions of the left before describing their scorching wind and boiling water; this gives the contrasting group's adverse outcome.

Jacob's eyes whiten from grief (وَابْيَضَّتْ عَيْنَاهُ مِنَ الْحُزْنِ); this is a distinct eye-state from the section's anger-swelling and coolness, but specifically shows emotion registered in the eyes.

God tells Musa and Harun to speak gently to Pharaoh (قَوْلًا لَيِّنًا); this is the softness side of the section's dictionary contrast, using a different root, and addresses the same speakers as its anger narrative.
By God's mercy, the Prophet is gentle with his companions and is told to pardon and seek forgiveness for them; it gives a concrete soft-and-forgiving stance opposite harshness.
